title: Acne: caring for your skin and choosing treatment
intro: Acne involves blocked hair follicles and inflammation. It can produce blackheads, whiteheads, inflamed spots and deeper painful lumps, often on the face, chest or back. It is not a sign of poor hygiene. The best plan depends on the kind of spots, scarring risk, previous treatment and how the condition affects your life.

sections.heading: Understand the changes in your skin
paragraphs: Skin oil and shed skin cells can collect inside follicles. Inflammation and the activity of bacteria normally present on the skin contribute to some spots. Hormonal changes can increase oil production, so acne is common during adolescence but can continue or begin in adulthood. A blackhead's colour does not mean there is dirt inside it. Acne is not contagious, and scrubbing cannot remove its underlying cause.

sections.heading: Use a routine you can maintain
paragraphs: Gentle cleansing and products labelled non-comedogenic can help you avoid additional irritation or blocked pores. Picking or squeezing spots increases the risk of marks and scars. Expensive products and a complicated routine are not automatically better. Tell a pharmacist or clinician about every product you already use: combining several irritating treatments can make skin sore and make it difficult to work out what is helping.

sections.heading: Discuss the available treatment options
paragraphs: Options can include benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids and other medicines applied to the skin. Some people need prescription tablets or specialist care. Antibiotics are used selectively because of side effects and resistance; they are not a reason to use leftover tablets. Isotretinoin needs specialist supervision and important safety precautions. Tell your prescriber if you are pregnant, could become pregnant or are planning pregnancy, because some acne medicines are unsuitable.

sections.heading: Judge progress without expecting an overnight change
paragraphs: Treatment takes time, and irritation or dryness can occur before the full benefit is apparent. Ask what changes to expect, how to use the chosen product and when to review it. A brief note or occasional photograph, kept privately, can help you describe changes without checking your skin constantly. Persistent dark or light marks are different from new inflamed spots and may need a separate discussion.

sections.heading: Seek help for scarring, pain or distress
paragraphs: Consult a clinician for deep painful lumps, developing scars, an uncertain diagnosis or acne that is not improving with an agreed plan. Rapidly worsening painful swelling with fever needs prompt assessment rather than stronger acne products. Embarrassment, bullying and withdrawing from activities also deserve attention. You do not have to wait until the skin looks severe before asking for emotional support or treatment advice.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: simplifying a routine
examples.text: A student uses a scrub, an acid toner and an acne gel, and their skin stings. They bring the product names to a pharmacist and ask which combination is appropriate. This helps identify irritation and clarify a plan; it does not guarantee that a particular product will clear the acne.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: asking about scars
examples.text: Someone notices deeper lumps and new indentations despite using their prescribed treatment. They arrange a review and explain how the acne affects their confidence. They ask whether specialist referral is appropriate instead of squeezing the lumps or buying another strong treatment.

questions: Which type of acne do I have, and is there a risk of scarring?
How should I use this treatment, and which side effects or pregnancy precautions matter?
When should we review progress, and what would change the plan?
